post.text:
GENIUS ISN'T CHEAP. 💸

The last 24h in superintelligence:
- Altman: AI is now mostly smarter than top scientists
- Anthropic: nearly $17B in sales in 3 months
- Marvell buys Lumentum for $115B
- Robots race up Mount Tai with eggs

Who should foot the bill?
post.alt: A 3-minute, fast-cut motion-graphics showreel of the last day in superintelligence (3 Nov 2026), hosted by Claudia: Sam Altman saying AI is now mostly smarter than top scientists, Anthropic's nearly $17 billion quarter and $895 billion in compute commitments, Grok Bot's costs, OpenAI's grid pledge, Marvell's $115 billion Lumentum deal, South Korea's AI budget, ADNOC's OpenAI agents, US data-centre votes, OpenAI's everyday-errands test, hidden deepfake apps, Goldman's AI coding limits, robots racing up Mount Tai and Japan's rules for cars with no steering wheel, with captions, sources and screenshots of the news articles.

stories.title: Sam Altman: AI is now mostly smarter than our smartest scientists
stories.summary: Opening ADIPEC in Abu Dhabi, OpenAI's Sam Altman said AI was mostly not as smart as our smartest scientists at the start of this year and is now mostly smarter than them. 'Atoms are still atoms,' he added: powering it will dominate the cost.

stories.title: Anthropic's IPO filing: nearly $17B in quarterly sales and $895.4B in commitments
stories.summary: Anthropic's amended IPO filing shows nearly $17B in revenue in the third quarter, about 12 times a year earlier, and $895.4B committed to purchases, almost all computing and infrastructure, with about $448B due by the end of 2030 (Bloomberg).

predictions.note: One lab's revenue reached nearly $17B in a single quarter, about 12 times a year earlier: still far below a national government's revenue, but climbing fast.

stories.title: Musk: serving Grok Bot cost 'unsustainably high relative to revenue'
stories.summary: After some Grok Bot users found their weekly limits suddenly maxed out over Halloween weekend, Elon Musk said in a reply on X that the cost of serving it 'was unsustainably high relative to revenue'. He hasn't said how the limits will change.

stories.title: OpenAI's Grid Protectors: its data centres will ease off when the grid is strained
stories.summary: OpenAI's Grid Protectors Program starts at its Georgia campus, where Georgia Power can cut up to 1,000 MW, about the average demand of 700,000 homes, when the grid is strained. 'Families and small businesses should not be asked to subsidize' its power, OpenAI says.

predictions.note: OpenAI will let Georgia Power cut up to 1,000 MW from its campus when the grid is strained, so households don't subsidise its power: one company's voluntary step.

stories.title: Marvell to buy laser maker Lumentum for $115B
stories.summary: Chipmaker Marvell agreed to buy Lumentum, which makes lasers and optical components for AI data centres, in an all-stock deal valued at $115B including debt (equity value $102.54B), Reuters reports. It's expected to close in the first half of 2028.

stories.title: South Korea plans to double AI and chip spending in 2027, to about $16B
stories.summary: In his 2027 budget speech, South Korea's President Lee said spending on AI and chips will double to a record 21.3 trillion won (about $16B), AFP reports. It's a proposal: parliament still has to pass the budget.

stories.title: ADNOC becomes the first energy company to deploy OpenAI Frontier, with G42
stories.summary: Abu Dhabi's ADNOC signed a multi-year deal with OpenAI and G42 to use AI agents across its operations, starting with oil and gas field development plans it hopes will take hours instead of months, with human experts overseeing the major decisions.

predictions.note: An energy major is handing field-planning work to AI agents while its human experts oversee the major decisions: one company's plan, not yet the norm.

stories.title: US voters in dozens of towns decide on data-centre bans and pauses
stories.summary: In Tuesday's US elections, voters in dozens of towns decide on banning or pausing data centres: Fortune counts 41 measures in 10 states, amid fights over power bills, while HuffPost counts dozens of municipalities in at least seven states.

predictions.note: Dozens of US towns are voting on banning or pausing data centres amid fights over power bills: a local version of data centres becoming a political constraint.

stories.title: OpenAI's everyday-errands test: GPT-6 Astra scores 80%, up from 49.3% for GPT-5.2
stories.summary: OpenAI's new test of everyday tasks, built from a survey of about 4,000 ChatGPT users, scores GPT-6 Astra at 80% against 49.3% for last year's GPT-5.2, including 93.1% on finding the right kindergarten after a move. These are OpenAI's own results.

stories.title: WIRED: 400+ ordinary-looking AI apps and sites hide abusive deepfake tools
stories.summary: WIRED found a network of more than 400 connected apps and websites, such as a 'pet portrait' app, that cloak sexually abusive deepfake features to pass app store review. AppleInsider reports Apple has removed 19 of the apps.

stories.title: Goldman Sachs limits AI coding tools to its engineers, Bloomberg reports
stories.summary: Goldman Sachs bankers and traders had been using Claude Code and GitHub; internal guidance updated in October now limits them to engineers after a review of productivity and risk, according to Bloomberg.

stories.title: Robots race up China's Mount Tai, some carrying eggs and watermelons
stories.summary: About 90 teams raced robots up Mount Tai's 3,000-plus steps in the World Mountain Robot Challenge. A robot dog from Unitree subsidiary Beijing Lingyi Technology finished in 43 min 41 s; most tourists take at least two hours, AFP reports.

stories.title: Japan weighs safety rules for self-driving cars with no steering wheel or pedals
stories.summary: Japan is considering revising its auto safety certification standards to cover self-driving vehicles without steering wheels, brakes or accelerator pedals, Nikkei Asia reports. Nothing has been decided yet.

transcript.t: It's Tuesday, November 3, and this is the Singularity Daily.
Let's catch you up on the last 24 hours in superintelligence.
Genius isn't cheap.
Sam Altman says AI is now mostly smarter than our smartest scientists.
But atoms are still atoms, he said. Power will decide what it costs.
Anthropic's filing to go public shows almost $17 billion in sales, in just three months.
But it's also promised to spend nearly $900 billion, mostly on computing power.
Meanwhile, Elon Musk says Grok Bot got too expensive to run.
Users are hitting their limits.
OpenAI says its new data centres will ease off when the grid's strained.
Families shouldn't pay.
Now, the big bets.
Chipmaker Marvell is buying laser maker Lumentum, for $115 billion.
South Korea's president says it'll double AI and chip spending next year, to about $16 billion.
Abu Dhabi's oil giant signed up for OpenAI's agents.
Its hope? Oil field plans in hours, not months.
And on Tuesday, Americans in dozens of towns vote on banning or pausing data centres.
Meanwhile, OpenAI built a test for everyday errands.
Last year's model scored 49%. This year's? 80%.
Like finding the right kindergarten after a move, or a meal plan for a parent with diabetes.
The catch? WIRED found over 400 apps and sites hiding abusive deepfake tools.
And Goldman Sachs pulled AI coding tools from its bankers. Engineers only.
So... is it so over?
We're so back!
Now, robots. About 90 teams raced them up China's sacred Mount Tai, some carrying eggs and watermelons.
A robot dog finished the climb in under 44 minutes.
Most tourists take two hours.
And Japan is weighing rules for self-drivin g cars with no steering wheel and no pedals.
So, genius isn't cheap. The real question is who pays, and whether it pays us back.
Zoom out, and the line only goes up.
Every day, the future shows up a little earlier.
All of that, in one day. And the days keep getting bigger.
You've been watching the Singularity Daily.
Go build something. See you tomorrow.
Want the whole month? Hear more on November 27.
